titulo: In ancient Rome, overcharging for a sausage could get you executed 🏛️
descripcion: Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices (301 AD) capped over a thousand prices, with the death penalty. Spoiler: it didn't work. Series: How Empires Fall. Full video: https://youtu.be/wsfUYT8hl7Q

escenas.texto: In the year three oh one, in Rome, overcharging for a sausage could cost you your life.
Emperor Diocletian set maximum prices for over a thousand products: beef, wine, shoes, even wages.
Why? Because for decades, emperors had been mixing copper into their silver coins to pay the army, and prices exploded.
Did it work? No. It was enforced unevenly, the limits weren't respected, and within about four years it was mostly ignored.
What did work was a stable gold coin: Constantine's solidus, which stayed the same for centuries.
The lesson: price controls fight the symptom. The cause was the money. Follow for the series: how empires fall.
